title: '我想做一档自己愿意看的节目'——Galaxies 如何在拥挤的发布会生态中找到位置
content:
"I wanted to make the show I wanted to watch" – How Galaxies found a place in the crowded showcase landscape | GamesIndustry.biz

Tomorrow will see the debut of the fourth
Galaxies Showcase
, which has managed to carve out a space of its own in the increasingly crowded lineup of digital showcases that have blossomed since the pandemic. Its indie and double-A lineup occupies a careful middle ground between the purely-digital indie collaborations at the bottom of the market and Geoff Keighley's top-dollar showcase at the top – with platform-led events like State of Play and Nintendo Direct occupying rarefied air alongside. Galaxies' pitch is a high-end studio production, anchored by Outside Xbox's Jane Douglas, delivering a tightly curated hour – and no more – of game trailers, mixing paid and free placements.
Galaxies founder Chris Thomas set out to "make the show that I would want to watch," he says, "which is one that's respectful of your time. I went to E3 for years and you'd go to the EA press conference – this is no slight on EA – and sit through 15 minutes of FIFA and NFL when I wanted to see, like, Mass Effect." His dream showcase was a high-quality production with what he describes as "tapas-style" variety of games: no asides or developer interviews, "and if there's a game on screen you don't care about, you only have to wait no more than 59 seconds to be served something else."
The approach has proved successful. The audience for the spring showcase – the event airs twice a year, in April and October, which Thomas says is the result of putting every other event in an Excel sheet and and seeing which gaps the show could "own" – more than doubled in its second year, not including social clips. GameDiscoverCo data says that it drove an average wishlist gain of +17,731.
This represents a gamble paying off for Thomas, who launched Galaxies as a bootstrapped project after a ten-year stint leading video game sales at Twitch's UK office, and before that sales roles at Gamespot UK and Videogamer. The experience left him with an abundance of professional and personal connections, including former GameSpot colleagues Douglas and Seb Ford, who runs games-focused production house DoubleJump. He also knew the shortcomings of the other showcases, from the games marketeers he spoke to every day.
Chris Thomas |
Image credit:
Galaxies Showcase
"I kept hearing the same things: first-party showcases are invite-only so you can't plan around them. Other major showcases are too expensive. And I realized I'd been at Twitch for ten years, it's a good innings, I should probably start to think about something else. And I realised I'm uniquely positioned to do this because I've got all these client contacts. My best friend Seb, who I've known since I was four, has a video production company. I know Jane from our GameSpot days together. I've got all the pieces to have a stab at this. And if I don't do it, who's going to have a go at it? That was it, really."
"And then it was: how can we be as disruptive as possible and as loud about it as we can, which basically just was me posting on LinkedIn every damn day and being a real pain in the ass to everyone." The enterprise was, and remains, a lean operation: Thomas led sales and his partner, Ari Raad, served as curator for the games in the show.
Even with such advantages, the first showcase was a dice roll. "It was a big gamble," says Thomas. "I'd left Twitch, we'd just moved house, I had a little bit of money left over, and it was
just
enough to pay for the recording of the show," which took place in a small studio in Croydon.
"They didn't ask for any money, which was great, because we didn't have any"
There was enough left in the kitty for a single paid co-stream, from CohhCarnage, but the pitch was strong enough to land a number of other streamers as well. "We worked with Streamers Connected who were brilliant, and they just wanted to be involved. They didn't ask for any money, which was great, because we didn't have any. I think they just thought it was a cool idea and they wanted to get behind it. They came on board and whipped up some co-streamers, and we put a signup form for other Twitch co-streamers on our website. By the end of the first show we had 120."
Then it was just a case of signing up the games, which he describes as "basically just me pulling every favour I had accrued over the years." Konami, Remedy, Krafton, Kepler, and Team17 signed up, and the lineup included new Expedition 33 gameplay and Twitch drops for Black Desert Online. They were won over by what Thomas describes as "take-a-punt-on-it-pricing", and what may be described as transparent uncertainty. "People would ask how many views it was going to get, and I would say 'I have no idea. Your guess is literally as good as mine.' I would try and make it very clear that if this is a high risk for you, then don't do it. But no one backed down."
After months of work, the show finally debuted in March 2025, exclusively on Twitch. This decision was practical rather than strategic. "I knew Twitch inside out," says Thomas, "and I didn't have a relationship with YouTube." The event was co-streamed by IGN (which is operated by IGN Entertainment, the parent company of
GamesIndustry.biz
).
Outside Xbox's Jane Douglas hosts each show, which is pre-recorded. |
Image credit:
Galaxies Showcase
It worked, in no small part because Asmongold noticed the show and co-streamed it, adding a seven-figure view count across Twitch and YouTube. "We hit 23,000 concurrents or something like that, my phone blew up with messages from old colleagues and I was just in a trance state. It was surreal, after six months of work and gambling everything."
